newsitem.title: NORTH KOREA: Ground broken in N.Korea for nuclear project.
newsitem.headline: Ground broken in N.Korea for nuclear project.

text.p: A consortium of capitalist nations broke ground on Tuesday for a landmark nuclear project in communist North Korea that Washington and Seoul have said is key to preserving peace on the peninsula.

Puffs of pink, green, orange and yellow smoke belched from a hillside in the northeastern town of Kumho as officials of the Korean Peninsula Energy Development Organisation (KEDO) triggered a "symbolic blast".

KEDO is an international consortium, led by the United States, South Korea and Japan, responsible for financing the construction of two 1,000-megawatt light-water reactors in North Korea at an estimated cost of $4.5 billion to $5 billion.
The reactors are to be delivered in return for Pyongyang's 1994 promise to freeze and eventually dismantle its suspected atomic weapons programme.
Witnesses said diplomats from nine nations and the European Union put on white gloves and released a barrage of confetti and streamers as fireworks cascaded from the hillside.
They were among 200 people at the ground-breaking ceremony, which also included journalists and South Korean contractors.
Stephen Bosworth, the U.S. executive director of KEDO, said Tuesday's ceremony had political importance because it would help establish the consortium's credibility.

"This ground-breaking ceremony...marks the fulfilment of a promise -- a promise made over two years ago by the Republic of Korea, Japan and the United States," Bosworth said at the start of the ceremony.

"As we are all aware, the light-water reactor project was initiated to help ensure the peace and security of a denuclearised and war-free Korean peninsula," said Chang Sun-sup, chief South Korean representative for the project.
"It is the promising product of a concerted international effort to realise these ideals on the Korean peninsula."

KEDO, formed in 1995 by Washington, Seoul and Tokyo under a U.S.-North Korean agreement in 1994, was later expanded to include Australia, Canada, Chile, Finland, Indonesia, New Zealand and the European Union.
Chang said Tuesday's ground-breaking served as "a catalyst for reconciliation and cooperation" with the reclusive North.
South Korea, which is paying for most of the project, brought to Kumho 9,000 tonnes of earth-moving equipment which roared to life when the symbolic blast went off.
Bosworth told reporters that the project was "a bargain" in view of the international community's gains.

The West had suspected that Pyongyang had secured enough plutonium to build one or two nuclear bombs and could try to sell them to a terrorist group to earn the hard currency needed to rescue the impoverished state from an economic crisis.

Before KEDO puts the reactor cores in the new reactors, to be built over the next seven to 10 years, the International Atomic Energy Agency, the U.N. nuclear watchdog, must be satisfied that North Korea has no weapons-grade plutonium.

"They have to come clean before they get the guts of the reactors," said Joel Wit, deputy director of the U.S. State Department's Office of Korean Affairs. "If they don't come clean, they get a concrete building and that's it," he added.

Under the U.S.-North Korean agreement signed in Geneva in October 1994, North Korea pledged to allow the IAEA to conduct special inspections of all its nuclear facilities to determine it had not hidden any weapons-grade plutonium that could be used to make a nuclear bomb.

Western officials have said in the past that they suspected North Korea might have secretly secured up to 10 kilos of fissile materials from its experimental graphite-moderated reactor, which it has since agreed to dismantle.

Seoul officials said they hoped the "historic" project would help lead to further cooperation between Seoul and Pyongyang, which have been locked in a Cold War confrontation since the 1950-53 Korean War.
